slides: Okay, before you practice, here's a quick summary of lines and angles.
All the rules, one at a time.
All the angles around one point add up to three hundred sixty degrees.
A straight line is half of that. A hundred eighty.
Smaller than ninety? That's acute. Bigger than ninety? Obtuse.
A right angle is ninety degrees. Two perpendicular lines make it.
On the exam, there's almost always a dot in the middle of the square.
Now, looks like ninety? That's not enough. It has to be marked, or given.
Two angles side by side on one straight line add up to a hundred eighty. Forty-seven next to x? Then x is a hundred thirty-three.
When two lines cross, the angles facing each other are equal.
And a bisector splits an angle into two equal halves.
Parallel lines and a transversal give you eight angles. Four small, and four large.
All the small ones are equal. And all the large ones are equal.
And a small one plus a large one is always a hundred eighty.
See parallel lines? Look for the Z. The two angles in its corners are equal.
And two angles inside a U, on the same side, between the lines, add up to a hundred eighty. Like fifty-three and a hundred twenty-seven.
Two lines perpendicular to the same line are parallel. And so are two lines parallel to the same line.
Now, lines can look parallel. Don't trust your eyes.
Nothing given? Look for a rule in the figure that proves it. A U that adds up to a hundred eighty, for example.
Four points on a line. AC and BD overlap on BC. So twelve plus nine, minus the whole sixteen... BC is five.
And seven equally spaced points make six gaps, not seven.
So, before you start, always ask yourself these questions.
And the traps: trusting the picture, and counting points instead of gaps.
Okay, now it's your turn. Good luck.
